Aqua Safety - preventing drowning

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...prevent your child form becoming another drowning statistic.

Summary:
Drowning remains one of the top causes of unnatural childhood death in South Africa. According to recent statistics released by private hospital group Netcare, nearly 72% of near-drownings occur around the home and only 1.22% at the beach. Three-year-old children seem particularly vulnerable and constitute 45.45% of the total. Furthermore, for every child that dies from drowning, five are left with permanent brain damage from the lack of oxygen that occurs in a near-drowning. With summer approaching, many more children are set to drown this year. There are many measures that can be introduced to make pools and bodies of water safe, but one of the best options is to teach children to survive when falling into water. We visit a swimming pool where babies and toddlers (from 6 months upwards) are taught to survive and float for at least 15 minutes after falling in a pool fully clothed with a winter jacket on. Check out the following YouTube videos: http://youtu.be/UBUTY85e8k0, http://youtu.be/lQaVNMJVW_s



Further information:
The Government Employees Medical Scheme (GEMS) writes on their website: "Every day more than one child drowns in South Africa. Over a third of these drownings are children under the age of fourteen years. The Medical Research Council consistently lists drowning as the third-highest cause of accidental deaths in children under the age of five, with only pedestrian motor vehicle accidents and shack fires being higher risks.
Most drowning and near-drowning incidents happen when a child falls into a pool, or is left alone in the bath. Sixty to 90 percent of drownings occur in residential pools and this is a statistic that parents cannot afford to ignore. Although the death statistics with regards to drowning are shocking, the consequences of near-drownings are even more so. For every child that dies from drowning, five suffer from permanent brain damage as a result of a near-drowning. It takes only four minutes without oxygen for irreversible brain damage to occur. We encourage all child minders to be extra vigilant if children have access to swimming pools, ponds or any other body of water. 90% of children who drown are under some sort of supervision at the time. This proves that, in spite of good intentions, no parent is able to protect their child from drowning by ‘keeping an eye open'. It is irresponsible of parents to not do all they possibly can to keep their children safe." GEMS then continues to list water safety measures, but fail to mention teaching children to swim/float. This insert is showing that it is possible to quickly and effectively teach even babies how to survive in water. We will visit one such swim school in Pretoria that follows the method pioneered by Jean Fouace of Switzerland. It is called "Bebes Amphibies". It started in 1967 when his son was playing at the pool side in a holiday resort, when he was called away to the telephone, needless to say the child decided to get a closer look at the water… and SPLASH! … Seconds later his father saw what happened and noticed he had his mouth tightly closed and his eyes wide open. The pool attendant, surprised to see his father observing the child, jumped into the water to rescue the child… The adventure started there, Jean decided he was going to work on a method of teaching babies and young children the self-survival skills of turning onto their back to ﬂoat with their respiratory tracts out of the water, after a lot of research and practice his method teaches babies and children a conditioned reﬂex that can their lives. Jean has trained hundreds of teachers worldwide with his method to help prevent children from drowning by teaching them conditioned self-survival reﬂexes.The owner of the swim school has worked extensively with Jean and has a large number of children in her school. She will provide us with good case studies and show us how it works. Important info at the beginning of summer. Check out the following YouTube videos: http://youtu.be/UBUTY85e8k0, http://youtu.be/lQaVNMJVW_s

Press Release:


Amphibian Babies
A remarkable technique now uses infants’ own natural reflexes to help save their lives in situations where they could have drowned. Carte Blanche witnesses the marvel of babies learning to calmly float in deep water for up to 15 minutes - until help arrives.


Script:


Devi:
A parent’s worst nightmare. An unattended baby or toddler falling into a pool. But watch what happens. You will not believe your eyes.

Devi:
That’s astonishing! Although that was an re-enactiment, it does prove the point that children, who can barely walk, can be taught to save themselves if they fall into water.

V/O:
This baby is just 7 months old and is learning how to survive in water.

And this one is not much older. She can actually fall into the water and roll over by herself so that she is floating on her back and breathing…..

The instructor who is teaching the children these skills is Lizette Botha. She owns a swimming school in Pretoria.

In addition to giving normal swimming lessons to children, she also takes in babies and teaches them to survive in water and float on their backs for as long as 15 minutes at a time.

Devi:
How long have you been in the business?

Lizette:
I’v been doing normal swimming lessons for 27 years and the baby floating for 24 years.

Devi:
So let us go back 24 years. How were you trained in this particular technique?

Lizette:
It actually starte with Juan village, the founder of this method, in 1967 when he was in Switzerland and his child fell in. He was only 9 months and he saw it.

V/O:
Jean observed his child under the water, eyes open and mouth closed. He was not swallowing water. A natural reflex had kicked in. Up to the age of about 18 months, a baby's epiglottis will automatically close over and block the throat when the child is submerged in water.

Lizette:
It’s a natural instinct that all babies have from birth because they come out of the mom’s womb. So it’s natural.

V/O:
This reflex protects infants in water. In addition, infants naturally float horizontally in water. If they can then be taught to roll onto their backs, they can survive. On this basis Jean developed a program and Lizette’s is following the methodology.

Lizette:
If they do this floating process that I’m doing, they fall in, it locks the airways so no water can go to the lungs or stomach. They open their eys so they know where they ar, immediately they turn around so that they can survive.

V/O:
In her school Lizette starts with babies as young as 6 months old.

LINK:
This may seem extremely young but one can’t overemphasize the importance of water safety. The statistics around drowning in South Africa are horrendous.

Dave:
Drowning is definitely a big problem for children in South Africa. In the summer months more than half of our drowings occur. I wouldn’t say on a daily basis but it is a regular occurrence.

V/O:
Dave Stanton is the Campus Manager for the Netcare 911’s Education Facility and he says that many drowning incidents occur in home swimming pools.

Dave:
Your home swimming pool is definitely an unsaf place, particularly if it doesn’t have a poolnet or a fence around it. We see many many drownings of children in home swimming pools and things like fishponds.

V/O:
Adriaan Kruger nearly became one of these sad statistics a few months ago. We met him, his mother Mart Mari and little sister Esti at their home in Pretoria.

Devi:
Tell me what happened that day.

Mart Mari:
It was a Friday afternoon. I was at home with Adriaan and my mom and I was waiting for my husband to get home because he had to look after Adriaan that night. I had a function at school.

V/O:
Her husband got home as she was about to leave.

Mart-Mari:
Then he had to go to the garage to get some stuff there and he was thinking that Adriaan was with me.

V/O:
Just before she left Mart-Mari looked out of a bedroom window.

Mart Mari:
I heard some funny noises outside. I was thinking it was probably the dog again but when I looked out it was like a choking and I saw something float on the water. And then it triggered my mind that it must be Adriaan because I saw the same movements that he made when he was at the swimming lessons.

V/O:
This is the swimming pool where it happened. Adriaan’s dad dived in and brought him out to safety.

But there are many other stories similar to Adriaan’s.

Cornis:
We have first-hand experience where out daughter of 2 years and 10 months fell into the pool and was able to actually save herself.
V/O:
Cornis Meintjies works from home and his daughter Lua is also one of Lizette’s floating babies. It was in this swimming pool at their home that tragedy nearly struck in November last year. Little Lua and her nanny Cynthia were playing in the yard.

Cornis:
When she ran around the swimming pool she was looking backwards, towards Cynthia’s direction and I think she missed the edge and she fell in about one and a half, two meters from the side of the pool.

V/O:
Then Lua’s self-survival lessons kicked in.

Cornis:
It was quite amazing. When Cynthia eventully got to her in a couple of seconds Lua went to the bottom of the pool and when she got there she saw that Lua was actually kicking herself upwards to the surface and swimming towards the side of the pool.

V/O:
Before her Nanny Cynthia could reach the pool, Lua had already got out and was safe.

Devi:
How do you feel the fact that your daugher, at 2 years and 10 months was able to save herself?

Cornis:
I still can’t believe it. All the time and efforts spent on the swimming classes and pool safety actually paid off.

V/O:
Mart-Mari agrees with Cornis that the lessons were worthwhile.

Mart Mari:
We wanted to stop with the lessonsbecause its real scary to take your child there and they cry the whole time. They don’t like the swimming lessons. But you know its so totally worth it. If I have to choose between a baby that’s crying and a child that’s still alive, I’d do it all over again.

V/O:
The lessons that Adriaan took ultimately ensured that Mart Mari still has a son to read to and that little Esti has a big brother to look up to.

V/O:
Dave Stanton says any measure that can buy a child time in water some time is to be recommended.

Dave Stanton
Anything that prevents a child from panicking and keeps them able to help themselves will definitely be very beneficial. If they can keep their head above water they're not going to drown. And then hopefully adults will notice them and pluck them out of the pool sooner.

V/O:
Lizette does not claim that her method guarantees a child’s survival, but it is one important weapon in an arsenal of measures that parents ought to employ to safeguard their children. These include adult supervision, fences, gates, nets and swimming lessons.

V/O:
At the swimming school many of the babies being taught were crying as they were taken into the water – that’s not easy for a parent to see.

Mart Mari:
Its real tough to see your baby crying when they're doing the lessons. It breaks your heart but if it saves their live that’s what you have to do.
